notes:
Work

  • $W = \vec F\cdot\vec d = Fd\cos\theta$. Work is zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement.
  • Work-energy theorem: the net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy, $W_{net} = \Delta KE$.

Energy

  • Kinetic energy $KE = \frac12mv^2 = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$ (so KE $\propto p^2$ at fixed mass).
  • Gravitational PE (near Earth) $= mgh$; elastic (spring) PE $= \frac12kx^2$.
  • Work done in stretching/compressing a spring from $x_1$ to $x_2$: $W = \frac12k(x_2^2-x_1^2)$.

Conservative vs non-conservative forces

ConservativeNon-conservative
Work independent of pathWork depends on path
Work over a closed path = 0Work over a closed path $\neq 0$
Gravity, spring force, electrostatic forceFriction, air drag

Power

  • $P = \dfrac{W}{t} = \vec F\cdot\vec v$; SI unit watt (W); 1 hp = 746 W.

Collisions (momentum is always conserved)

  • Elastic collision: KE is also conserved. For equal masses with one initially at rest, the velocities are completely exchanged.
  • Perfectly inelastic collision: the bodies stick together and move with a common velocity $v = \dfrac{m_1u_1+m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$; kinetic energy is lost (converted to heat, sound, deformation).
  • Coefficient of restitution $e = \dfrac{\text{relative velocity of separation}}{\text{relative velocity of approach}}$: $e=1$ for a perfectly elastic collision, $e=0$ for a perfectly inelastic one, $0

Exam tip

KCET sets 2–3 questions from this chapter, typically one work/energy numerical, one power numerical, and one collision (elastic or perfectly inelastic) problem. Always check whether momentum, KE, or both are conserved before solving a collision question.

questions.q: A force of 10 N acting on a body causes a displacement of 5 m in a direction making an angle of 60° with the force. The work done is
questions.explanation: $W = Fd\cos\theta = 10\times5\times\cos60^\circ = 50\times0.5 = 25$ J.
questions.trick: $W=Fd\cos\theta$ — always include the angle's cosine.

questions.q: The kinetic energy of a body of mass 2 kg moving with a speed of 10 m s$^{-1}$ is
questions.explanation: $KE = \frac12mv^2 = \frac12\times2\times100 = 100$ J.
questions.trick: $KE=\frac12mv^2$ — direct plug-in.

questions.q: A body of mass 1 kg, initially at rest, has 50 J of net work done on it. Its final speed is
questions.explanation: By the work-energy theorem, $W = \frac12mv^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{2W/m} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ m s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Work-energy theorem: $W=\frac12mv^2\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{2W/m}$.

questions.q: The gravitational potential energy of a 3 kg mass held 4 m above the ground (taking the ground as reference) is
questions.explanation: $PE = mgh = 3\times10\times4 = 120$ J.
questions.trick: $PE=mgh$ — direct plug-in.

questions.q: A spring of force constant 200 N m$^{-1}$ is compressed by 10 cm. The elastic potential energy stored is
questions.explanation: $PE = \frac12kx^2 = \frac12\times200\times(0.1)^2 = 100\times0.01 = 1$ J.
questions.trick: Spring PE: $\frac12kx^2$ — convert cm to m first.

questions.q: A machine does 100 J of work in 5 s. Its power is
questions.trick: $P=W/t$ — direct division.

questions.q: A force of 10 N acts on a body moving with a velocity of 5 m s$^{-1}$ in the same direction as the force. The instantaneous power delivered is
questions.explanation: $P = \vec F\cdot\vec v = Fv\cos0^\circ = 10\times5 = 50$ W.
questions.trick: $P=Fv\cos\theta$; same direction means $\cos\theta=1$.

questions.q: A body of mass $m$ falls freely from rest through a height of 20 m. Using energy conservation, its speed just before hitting the ground is
questions.explanation: $mgh = \frac12mv^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2\times10\times20} = \sqrt{400} = 20$ m s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Free fall energy shortcut: $v=\sqrt{2gh}$.

questions.q: A body of mass $m$ moving with velocity $u$ collides elastically head-on with an identical body of mass $m$ at rest. After the collision
options: the first body stops and the second moves off with velocity $u$
both bodies move together with velocity $u/2$
both bodies move with velocity $u$ in opposite directions
the first body continues with velocity $u$ and the second stays at rest
questions.explanation: For a 1-D elastic collision between equal masses with one initially at rest, momentum and KE conservation together force a complete velocity exchange: the moving body stops and the target moves off with speed $u$.
questions.trick: Equal-mass elastic collision, one at rest → velocities completely exchange.

questions.q: A body of mass 2 kg moving at 3 m s$^{-1}$ collides and sticks to a body of mass 3 kg at rest. Their common velocity after the collision is
questions.explanation: Momentum conservation: $v = \dfrac{m_1u_1+m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2} = \dfrac{2\times3+0}{5} = \dfrac{6}{5} = 1.2$ m s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Perfectly inelastic: $v=(m_1u_1+m_2u_2)/(m_1+m_2)$.

questions.q: The coefficient of restitution $e$ for a perfectly elastic collision is
questions.explanation: $e$ equals the ratio of relative velocity of separation to relative velocity of approach; for a perfectly elastic collision this ratio is exactly 1.
questions.trick: $e=1$ defines a perfectly elastic collision.

questions.q: A force whose work done in moving a particle between two points does not depend on the path taken is called a
questions.explanation: This path-independence (equivalently, zero work over any closed loop) is the defining property of a conservative force, e.g. gravity or spring force.
questions.trick: Path-independent work = conservative force, by definition.

questions.q: The work done by friction on a body that moves around and returns to its starting point (a closed path) is
questions.explanation: Friction always opposes the direction of motion, so it does negative work throughout the path; over a closed loop this does not cancel to zero, unlike a conservative force. This is why friction is non-conservative.
questions.trick: Friction always opposes motion → net work over a loop is negative, not zero.

questions.q: A spring of force constant 100 N m$^{-1}$ is stretched from 10 cm to 20 cm extension. The additional work done is
questions.trick: Spring work between two stretches: $W=\frac12k(x_2^2-x_1^2)$, not $\frac12k(x_2-x_1)^2$.

questions.q: A pump lifts 1000 kg of water through a height of 10 m in 10 s. The power of the pump is
questions.explanation: $P = \dfrac{mgh}{t} = \dfrac{1000\times10\times10}{10} = 10000\,\text{W} = 10$ kW.
questions.trick: Pump power: $P=mgh/t$.

questions.q: If the momentum of a body is doubled while its mass stays the same, its kinetic energy becomes
questions.explanation: $KE = p^2/2m$, so doubling $p$ (at constant $m$) increases $KE$ by a factor of $2^2 = 4$.
questions.trick: $KE\propto p^2$ at fixed mass → double $p$ quadruples $KE$.

questions.q: A body of mass $m$ moving with speed $u$ collides perfectly inelastically with an identical body of mass $m$ at rest. The percentage of the initial kinetic energy that is lost is
questions.explanation: Initial $KE = \frac12mu^2$; common velocity $v=u/2$, final $KE = \frac12(2m)(u/2)^2 = \frac14mu^2$. Loss $= \frac14mu^2$, which is $50\%$ of the initial KE.
questions.trick: Equal-mass perfectly inelastic collision always loses exactly 50% of KE.

questions.q: A block of mass 4 kg moving at 5 m s$^{-1}$ is brought to rest by friction. The magnitude of the work done by friction is
questions.explanation: By the work-energy theorem, work done by friction $= \Delta KE = 0 - \frac12\times4\times25 = -50$ J; magnitude $50$ J.
questions.trick: Work by friction = $\Delta KE$ (negative, since it removes KE); take magnitude.

questions.q: The work done by a conservative force on a particle that moves around any closed path and returns to its starting point is
questions.explanation: Zero net work over every closed path is the defining property of a conservative force.
questions.trick: Zero work over any closed loop is the hallmark of a conservative force.

questions.q: 1 horsepower (hp) is equal to
questions.explanation: By definition, 1 hp $= 746$ W.
questions.trick: Memorise: 1 hp = 746 W.

questions.q: A machine takes in 500 J of energy and produces 400 J of useful output work. Its efficiency is
questions.explanation: Efficiency $= \dfrac{\text{output}}{\text{input}}\times100 = \dfrac{400}{500}\times100 = 80\%$.
questions.trick: Efficiency = output/input $\times100$.

questions.q: A force acting on a body varies linearly with displacement, from 0 to 20 N, as the body moves 5 m (the F-x graph is a straight line through the origin). The work done is
questions.explanation: Work $=$ area under the F-x graph $= \frac12\times5\times20 = 50$ J.
questions.trick: Linear F-x graph: work = area of triangle = $\frac12\times$base$\times$height.

questions.q: A body of mass 1 kg moving at 6 m s$^{-1}$ collides elastically head-on with a stationary body of mass 2 kg. The velocity of the 2 kg body after the collision is
questions.trick: Elastic collision, target initially at rest: $v_2'=2m_1u_1/(m_1+m_2)$.

questions.q: The potential energy of a particle moving along the x-axis is $U(x) = 5x^2$ J (x in metres). The magnitude of the force acting on it at $x=2$ m is
questions.trick: $F=-dU/dx$ — differentiate potential energy and negate.

questions.q: A 2 kg block is pushed up a frictionless incline of length 5 m inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The work done against gravity is ($g=10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.explanation: Height gained $= L\sin\theta = 5\times0.5 = 2.5$ m. $W = mgh = 2\times10\times2.5 = 50$ J.
questions.trick: Work against gravity depends only on height gained: $W=mgL\sin\theta$, not on incline length alone.

questions.q: A ball dropped from a height of 5 m rebounds to a height of 1.25 m. The coefficient of restitution between the ball and the floor is
questions.trick: Coefficient of restitution from heights: $e=\sqrt{h_2/h_1}$.

questions.q: A spring of force constant 200 N/m, compressed by 0.1 m, is released against a 0.5 kg block resting on a frictionless surface. The speed of the block as it leaves the spring is
questions.explanation: $\frac12kx^2 = \frac12mv^2 \Rightarrow v = x\sqrt{k/m} = 0.1\sqrt{400} = 2$ m s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Spring energy to KE: $v=x\sqrt{k/m}$.

questions.q: A car experiences a constant resistive force of 500 N while moving at a constant velocity of 20 m s$^{-1}$. The power delivered by its engine is
questions.explanation: At constant velocity, driving force equals resistive force: $P = Fv = 500\times20 = 10000$ W $= 10$ kW.
questions.trick: Constant velocity → driving force = resistive force; $P=Fv$.

questions.q: A small ball just completes a vertical circular loop of radius 2 m. Its minimum speed at the top of the loop is ($g=10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.explanation: At the minimum condition, gravity alone provides the centripetal force: $mg = mv^2/r \Rightarrow v=\sqrt{gr}=\sqrt{20}\approx4.47$ m s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Minimum speed at loop top: gravity alone supplies centripetal force, $v=\sqrt{gr}$.

questions.q: An engine does 3000 J of work in 1 minute. Its power output is
questions.trick: $P=W/t$ — remember to convert minutes to seconds.

questions.q: Energy is defined as the capacity of a body to do
questions.explanation: Energy is the ability of a system to perform work; it is measured in the same unit as work (joule).
questions.trick: Energy = capacity to do work, by definition.

questions.q: For a body of fixed mass, a graph of kinetic energy (KE) versus momentum (p) is
options: a straight line through the origin
questions.explanation: Since $KE = p^2/2m$, KE varies as the square of $p$, giving a parabola (with $m$ fixed).
questions.trick: $KE=p^2/2m$ is quadratic in $p$ → KE-vs-$p$ graph is a parabola.

questions.q: A 5 kg block slides down a frictionless incline, descending a vertical height of 3 m. The work done on it by gravity is ($g=10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.explanation: $W = mgh = 5\times10\times3 = 150$ J, regardless of the incline's angle or length.
questions.trick: Gravity's work depends only on vertical height dropped: $W=mgh$.

questions.q: In an elastic collision between two identical balls, one initially at rest, if the collision is not head-on (oblique), the angle between their velocity directions after the collision is
questions.explanation: For an oblique elastic collision between equal masses with one initially at rest, conservation of momentum and kinetic energy together force the two final velocity vectors to be perpendicular (90°).
questions.trick: Oblique elastic collision, equal masses, target at rest → final velocities always perpendicular (90°).

questions.q: The power rating (in watts) marked on an electrical appliance indicates
options: the rate at which it consumes (or delivers) energy
the voltage at which it operates
the total energy it can store
questions.explanation: Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy, $P=W/t$; the wattage tells you energy used per second.
questions.trick: Wattage = rate of energy use/delivery, not efficiency or voltage.

questions.q: A particle moving along the x-axis is acted on by a force $F = 3x^2$ N (x in metres). The work done in moving it from $x=0$ to $x=2$ m is
questions.explanation: $W = \int_0^2 3x^2\,dx = \left[x^3\right]_0^2 = 8$ J.
questions.trick: Variable force work = $\int F\,dx$ over the given limits.

questions.q: A pump lifts water at a rate of 50 kg per second through a height of 20 m. The power of the pump is ($g=10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.explanation: $P = \dfrac{dm}{dt}gh = 50\times10\times20 = 10000$ W $= 10$ kW.
questions.trick: Continuous pumping power: $P=(dm/dt)gh$.

questions.q: In uniform circular motion, the work done by the centripetal force on the particle is
questions.explanation: The centripetal force is always perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity, so $W = Fd\cos90^\circ = 0$ at every instant.
questions.trick: Centripetal force $\perp$ velocity always → does zero work.

questions.q: A 1 kg body is projected vertically upward with a kinetic energy of 100 J. The maximum height it reaches is ($g=10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.explanation: All KE converts to PE at the top: $mgh = 100 \Rightarrow h = 100/(1\times10) = 10$ m.
questions.trick: All KE converts to PE at max height: $h=KE/(mg)$.

questions.q: A stationary shell explodes into two fragments of masses 1 kg and 3 kg. The ratio of their kinetic energies (1 kg fragment : 3 kg fragment) is
questions.explanation: By momentum conservation the fragments have equal and opposite momenta ($p_1=p_2=p$). Since $KE=p^2/2m$, $KE_1:KE_2 = \dfrac{1}{m_1}:\dfrac{1}{m_2} = m_2:m_1 = 3:1$.
questions.trick: Explosion from rest: equal and opposite momenta → $KE\propto1/m$, so ratio is inverse of masses.
